# How to Improve Your ACT Science Score: 2026 Study Guide


## TL;DR


Improving your ACT Science score starts with learning how to interpret data, understand experiments, and answer questions efficiently under time pressure. You do not need to memorize an entire science textbook. Instead, focus on reading graphs accurately, identifying experimental variables, comparing scientific viewpoints, and reviewing the mistakes you make during practice.


This 2026 guide explains how to improve your ACT Science score with practical test-taking strategies, a targeted study plan, time-management techniques, and advice for deciding whether to take the optional Science section on the Enhanced ACT.


> **How Do You Improve Your ACT Science Score?**
>
>
> To improve your ACT Science score, take a timed diagnostic test, identify your weakest question types, and practice those skills with official ACT-style questions. Focus on interpreting graphs and tables, understanding experimental designs, comparing scientific viewpoints, and managing your time across the 40-question section. Review every incorrect answer to understand the mistake, then repeat targeted practice and take another timed test to measure your progress.
>
>
> The most effective approach is to combine accurate data interpretation, strategic question selection, and consistent timed practice rather than relying on memorizing large amounts of scientific information.


## What the ACT Science Section Actually Tests (and Why That Matters)


Here’s the single most important thing to understand: the ACT Science section is not really a science test. It’s a reading comprehension and data interpretation test dressed in a lab coat.


Even ACT’s own description confirms this. The test “emphasizes scientific reasoning skills over recall of scientific content,” and advanced knowledge of biology, chemistry, or physics is not required. Students who internalize this distinction tend to see the fastest score gains. One tutor writing on Substack reported that after just four sessions focused on reframing the section as data interpretation rather than science knowledge, a student jumped from a 26 to a 31, moving from the 85th to the 96th percentile.


If you’re wondering whether to invest time in this section at all, or how it fits into the bigger ACT picture, the format overview for the[full ACT test](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/act-test-format-sections-timing-scoring) is worth reading first.


The questions ask you to read graphs, identify trends, compare experimental setups, and evaluate competing scientific arguments. About four questions per test require actual science knowledge. The other 36 can be answered using nothing but what’s printed on the page in front of you.


**Ready to pinpoint exactly where you’re losing points?**[Try the ACT score predictor](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/predictor) to see which question types are holding your score back.


## ACT Science in the Enhanced ACT Format (2025-2026)


The ACT underwent a major restructuring starting in 2025. The Science section is now optional. This is not a minor tweak; it fundamentally changes how students should think about preparing for this section.


### Key Format Changes


Under the Enhanced ACT, if you choose to take Science, you’ll face 40 questions. The time limit has been extended to 40 minutes (up from 35 minutes in the legacy format). Some test prep sources still reference the old 35-minute limit, so double-check which format version any guide you’re reading refers to. Adding Science to your test costs an extra $4.


Your Science score (1-36) is reported separately. It no longer factors into your composite score, which is now calculated from English, Math, and Reading only.


### The STEM Score: A New Metric


Students who take the optional Science section also receive a STEM Score, which averages your Math and Science scaled scores. This is a new reporting category that most prep content hasn’t caught up to yet. For students applying to engineering, pre-med, or other STEM programs, this score could become a meaningful differentiator on applications, even if the composite no longer includes Science.


### Should You Take the Optional ACT Science Section?


Whether to take ACT Science depends on your target colleges, intended major, current preparation, and testing goals. Although Science is optional for the Enhanced ACT Composite score, some colleges or programs may require or recommend a Science score.


**Consider taking Science if:**


-


Your target college or program requires or recommends the section.


-


You are applying to a STEM-related program and want to report both Math and Science scores.


-


Your practice results suggest that you can earn a competitive Science score with additional preparation.


-


You want to keep your college application options open.


**Consider skipping Science if:**


-


Your target colleges do not require or recommend it.


-


Preparing for Science would take time away from improving your English, Math, or Reading scores.


-


Your current results and application goals do not justify taking the additional section.


Before registering, check the admissions requirements for each college and program on your list. Requirements can differ by institution, program, and application cycle, so do not rely on a general claim that most colleges treat Science the same way.


**Quick tip:** Create a list of your target colleges and record whether each school requires, recommends, or does not require ACT Science. Make your decision based on those policies rather than on a universal score cutoff.


For a broader look at what constitutes a competitive score, the guide to[good ACT scores](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/what-is-a-good-act-score-percentiles-ranges) breaks down percentile ranges by section.


## ACT Science Score Benchmarks: Where Do You Stand?


The ACT Science section is scored on a scale of 1–36. Your scaled score reflects your performance after ACT converts the number of scored questions you answer correctly. The conversion can vary by test form, so there is no single raw-score chart that applies to every administration.


Use these benchmarks to set a target for your preparation:


Science scaled score


What it means


20


A useful baseline for setting a personal improvement goal


23


ACT's Science College Readiness Benchmark


26


ACT's STEM College Readiness Benchmark, when considering the combined STEM score


28–32


A target range for students seeking stronger Science results


33–36


The highest score range


The Science benchmark of 23 represents the level associated with a 50% chance of earning a B or higher in a corresponding introductory college biology course. The STEM benchmark is 26 and applies to the combined Math and Science score, not the Science section alone.


To estimate your current performance, use the scoring key for the specific official practice test you complete. Then set your next target based on your scaled score, the questions you missed, and the requirements of your target colleges.


**Important:** Do not assume that a fixed number of correct answers always produces the same Science score. Use the scoring information for your particular test form.


For a detailed look at how raw scores convert to scaled scores across all sections, see the[ACT score chart guide](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/act-score-chart-raw-to-scaled-conversion) .


### What These Numbers Mean for Your Strategy


If you’re currently scoring a 20 and want a 28, you need roughly 10 more raw points. That’s 10 more correct answers out of 40. When you frame it that way, the gap feels manageable. Most of those 10 points will come from better time management and passage-type familiarity, not from learning more science.


## The Three Passage Types (and How to Handle Each One)


Every ACT Science section contains the same mix of passage types. Knowing what to expect removes the element of surprise and lets you allocate your time strategically.


### ACT Science Skills and the Best Strategy for Each


Skill area


What you need to do


Best approach


Interpretation of Data


Read graphs, tables, figures, and numerical results


Check labels, units, scales, and the exact data series referenced


Scientific Investigation


Understand experiments, variables, controls, and procedures


Identify what researchers changed, measured, and kept constant


Evaluating Scientific Evidence


Compare explanations, predictions, models, and experimental findings


Identify each claim and determine which evidence supports or challenges it


These skills overlap across ACT Science passages. Instead of memorizing a fixed passage count, learn to recognize the task each question requires. That makes your strategy more flexible when the layout or subject of a passage changes.


**A useful rule:** Find the relevant evidence first, interpret it carefully, and select the answer supported by the passage rather than by what you think should happen scientifically.


### Data Representation (2 passages, 25-35% of questions)


These passages present graphs, tables, scatter plots, and other visual data displays. The questions ask you to read values, identify trends, and sometimes interpolate or extrapolate from the data.


**Strategy:** Skim the passage text briefly, then go straight to the questions. The questions tell you exactly which figure or table to examine. Your job is to read the graphics accurately. Double-check axis labels, units, and scales. Most mistakes on these questions come from misreading a graph, not from lack of understanding.


These are typically the fastest passages to complete. Aim for 4-5 minutes per passage.


### Research Summaries (3 passages, 45-60% of questions)


These describe one or more experiments: what was set up, what was changed, and what was measured. They make up the largest chunk of the test.


**Strategy:** Focus on identifying the independent variable (what the researchers changed) and the dependent variable (what they measured). Note how different experiments in the same passage differ from each other. The questions frequently ask you to compare results across experiments or predict what would happen if a variable changed.


Budget about 5 minutes per passage. If you can quickly map out “they changed X, they measured Y, and here’s what happened,” most questions become straightforward.


### Conflicting Viewpoints (1 passage, 15-20% of questions)


This is the passage type that gives students the most trouble. It presents two or more scientists, students, or hypotheses that disagree about the same phenomenon. The questions test whether you can identify each viewpoint’s central claim and how the viewpoints differ.


**Strategy:** This passage requires actual reading, not just graph scanning. Write a brief summary (a few words or one sentence) of each viewpoint as you go. Distilling each position to its core claim lets you answer most questions without re-reading entire paragraphs.


Most prep experts recommend saving Conflicting Viewpoints for last. It requires closer reading than the other passage types, and attempting easier passages first builds confidence and banks time. Budget 6-7 minutes for this one.


To drill each passage type with targeted questions, the[ACT question bank](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/question-bank) lets you filter by question type so you can focus on your weak spots.


### The Field-Test Passage


The Enhanced ACT includes approximately 6 unscored field-test items embedded in the section. You won’t know which passage contains them. This means one of the passages you encounter doesn’t count toward your score, but since you can’t identify it, treat every passage as if it matters.


## ACT Science Question Types: A Complete Glossary


Understanding question types is just as important as understanding passage types. Here’s what you’ll encounter.


### Data Grab (Lookup) Questions


These ask you to find a specific value in a table or graph. “According to Figure 2, what was the temperature at 30 minutes?” They’re the easiest and fastest questions on the test.


**Tip:** Read axis labels carefully. The most common error is reading the wrong axis or the wrong data series.


### Trend and Pattern Questions


These ask about the direction or shape of a relationship. “As pressure increases, what happens to volume?” You need to identify whether a relationship is direct, inverse, or nonlinear.


**Tip:** Trace the data with your finger or pencil. If the line goes up to the right, the relationship is direct. Down to the right, inverse.


### ACT Science Practice Example: How to Read a Graph


Imagine a graph showing how plant height changes under three different amounts of daily light exposure.


Daily light exposure


Average plant height after 14 days


2 hours


5 cm


4 hours


9 cm


6 hours


12 cm


8 hours


12 cm


**Practice question:** Based on the data, what happens to average plant height as daily light exposure increases from 2 to 8 hours?


A. It decreases steadily.


B. It increases steadily at the same rate.


C. It increases and then levels off.


D. It remains unchanged.


**Correct answer: C. It increases and then levels off.**


**How to solve it:**


1.


Read the column headings and identify the measured outcome: average plant height.


2.


Compare the values as light exposure increases.


3.


Notice that height increases from 5 cm to 12 cm, then stays at 12 cm between 6 and 8 hours.


4.


Choose the answer that describes the complete pattern.


**ACT Science tip:** Do not choose an answer simply because the first few data points support it. Check the entire relevant trend, including any plateau, reversal, or exception.


### Interpolation and Extrapolation Questions


Interpolation asks you to estimate a value between two known data points. Extrapolation asks you to predict a value beyond the data range. Both require you to identify the trend and extend it logically.


**Tip:** For extrapolation, ask yourself whether the trend is linear or curved. Extending a curve as if it were a straight line is a common trap.


### Experimental Design Questions


These test whether you understand how experiments work: what’s being controlled, what’s being tested, why a control group exists. They often appear in Research Summary passages.


**Tip:** If a question asks “why did the scientists include Experiment 3,” look for what variable changed between experiments. The answer almost always relates to isolating a specific factor.


### Understanding Viewpoints Questions


Found exclusively in the Conflicting Viewpoints passage, these ask you to identify what a particular scientist or hypothesis would predict, agree with, or disagree with.


**Tip:** Refer back to your one-sentence summaries. If the question asks “Scientist 2 would most likely agree with which statement,” you need to match the answer choice to the core claim you wrote down.


### Outside Knowledge Questions


About four questions per test require background knowledge you won’t find in the passage. A comprehensive study of past ACT Science sections identified roughly 18 recurring topics. They span biology, chemistry, physics, and basic math.


Here’s the list worth reviewing:


-


**pH scale:** 0 is acidic, 14 is basic, 7 is neutral


-


**Phases of matter:** solid, liquid, gas; water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C


-


**Cell biology basics:** the nucleus stores DNA, mitochondria produce energy, chloroplasts handle photosynthesis


-


**Genetics:** dominant vs. recessive alleles, how to read a Punnett square


-


**Food chains and energy flow:** producers → consumers → decomposers; energy decreases at each level


-


**Kinetic vs. potential energy:** moving objects have kinetic energy; stored energy (height, springs, chemical bonds) is potential


-


**Scientific method terms:** independent variable, dependent variable, control group, hypothesis


-


**Basic chemistry:** atoms, elements, compounds, mixtures; the difference between physical and chemical changes


-


**Evolution basics:** natural selection, adaptation


-


**Earth science:** layers of the atmosphere, basic plate tectonics


-


**Density:** mass divided by volume; denser objects sink


-


**Electromagnetic spectrum:** radio waves to gamma rays, ordered by wavelength/frequency


-


**Acceleration and gravity:** objects in free fall accelerate at ~9.8 m/s²


You won’t need these for most questions, but knowing them guarantees you pick up 3-4 points that other students miss. That can be the difference between a 26 and a 28.


## Time Management: The Skill That Matters Most


Most students don’t lose points on ACT Science because they can’t understand the material. They lose points because they run out of time. This is the single biggest lever for improving your ACT Science score.


### How to Manage Your Time on ACT Science


The Enhanced ACT Science section gives you 40 minutes to answer 40 questions. That works out to an average of one minute per question, although some questions take only a few seconds while others require more careful analysis.


Use this approach to manage your time:


1.


**Start with a clear plan.** Quickly identify the passage format and the figures or experiments presented.


2.


**Answer direct questions efficiently.** Questions asking for a specific value or a straightforward comparison may take less time than questions requiring several steps of reasoning.


3.


**Avoid getting stuck.** If you cannot make progress after a reasonable attempt, eliminate clearly incorrect answers, select your best option if necessary, and move on.


4.


**Monitor your progress.** Check whether you are keeping pace with the number of questions remaining instead of spending too long on one difficult item.


5.


**Reserve time for unresolved questions.** If time permits, revisit flagged items and check your answer choices.


### Should You Answer ACT Science Passages in Order?


Not necessarily. Some students prefer starting with data-focused passages because they can quickly locate answers in graphs and tables. Others perform better when they follow the test's original order.


Try different approaches during practice and compare your accuracy and completion time. If you consistently lose time on one passage type, consider completing your strongest passages first.


The goal is not to follow a universal passage order. It is to answer as many questions accurately as possible within the time available.


### The “Now, Later, Never” Triage Method


Not all questions deserve your time equally. Use this three-bucket approach:


**Now:** Questions with clear locators (“According to Table 1…” or “Based on Figure 3…”). These are fast lookup questions. Answer them immediately.


**Later:** Questions that require synthesizing information across multiple figures or reading the passage introduction carefully. Flag these and come back after finishing the “Now” questions.


**Never:** If a question still stumps you after 30 seconds of focused effort on your second pass, pick your “letter of the day” and move on. There’s no penalty for wrong answers on the ACT, so never leave a question blank.


### Passage Order Strategy


You don’t have to work through passages in order. Practitioners on Reddit and prep forums consistently recommend this sequence:


1.


Data Representation passages first (fastest, highest confidence)


2.


Research Summaries second (moderate difficulty, most questions)


3.


Conflicting Viewpoints last (slowest, requires careful reading)


This front-loads the easy points and prevents you from spending 7 minutes on the hardest passage only to rush through three easier ones.

A structured study plan helps you turn ACT Science strategies into measurable progress. Instead of practicing every skill equally, focus first on the question types that cause the most errors.


This two-week plan assumes approximately 30–45 minutes of study per day. Adjust the schedule to fit your starting score, available time, and test date.

### How to Measure Your Progress


Track more than your total score. Record the number of questions answered correctly, the number left unanswered, the time spent, and the type of mistakes you made.


Look for three signs of improvement:


-


**Better accuracy:** You make fewer errors when reading data and interpreting experiments.


-


**Better pacing:** You finish more questions without rushing through the final passages.


-


**Better reasoning:** You can explain why the correct answer is supported by the evidence.


If your score does not improve after two weeks, do not automatically increase your study hours. First, determine whether your mistakes come from misunderstanding the data, misreading the question, weak background knowledge, or poor time management. Then adjust your practice accordingly.


A two-week plan is a starting point, not a guarantee of a particular score increase. Continue practicing until your results are consistent under timed conditions.


## Common Mistakes That Keep Scores Low


**Overthinking:** The ACT Science section rewards quick pattern recognition, not deep analysis. If you’re spending more than 30 seconds reasoning through a single question, you’re probably overthinking it.


**Reading every word of every passage:** You don’t need to. For Data Representation and Research Summaries, skim the text and let the questions guide you to the relevant figures. Only Conflicting Viewpoints demands careful reading.


**Ignoring units and labels:** A graph labeled in kilograms looks very different from one labeled in grams. Axis labels, units, and scales are where careless errors hide.


**Not practicing under time pressure:** Doing ACT Science questions untimed builds familiarity but not the speed you need on test day. Every practice session should involve a timer.


**Skipping the hardest questions entirely:** Remember, there’s no penalty for guessing. If you’re stuck, eliminate one or two answer choices and guess from the remaining options. Process of elimination turns a 25% chance into a 33% or 50% chance.


## Process of Elimination for ACT Science


Process of elimination (POE) is especially powerful on this section because many answer choices contain obviously wrong data readings. If the graph clearly shows an upward trend, any answer choice claiming a downward trend can be eliminated immediately.


For Conflicting Viewpoints questions, eliminate answers that blend the claims of different scientists. The test often includes answer choices that sound reasonable but actually combine Scientist 1’s position with Scientist 2’s evidence. If you’ve written your one-sentence summaries, these traps become obvious.


## How Long Does It Take to Improve Your ACT Science Score?


The timeline depends on your starting point and how consistently you practice. Students who are already scoring in the 22-26 range and just need strategy adjustments (time management, passage-type awareness, graph-reading precision) can often see 4-6 point gains in 2-4 weeks of focused daily practice.


Students starting below 20 typically need 4-8 weeks because they may need to build both strategy skills and background knowledge simultaneously.


The[ACT study plan guide](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/act-study-plan-step-by-step-guide) walks through how to structure your prep week by week, including how to allocate time across all four sections.


Practitioners on Reddit who have gone through the process report that the “paradigm shift” moment, when you stop treating it as a science test and start treating it as a data interpretation test, is when scores jump fastest. Everything after that is just practice and refinement.


## FAQ


### Is the ACT Science section still required?


No. As of the Enhanced ACT format introduced in 2025, Science is optional. It costs an additional $4 to add. Your Science score is reported separately and does not factor into your composite score. However, some colleges still require or recommend it, particularly for STEM applicants.


### What is a good ACT Science score?


The average is about 20 (50th percentile). The College Readiness Benchmark is 23, which suggests you’re prepared for introductory college science. For competitive STEM programs, aim for 28 or higher to reach the top 10 percent.


### How many questions can I miss and still get a 30 on ACT Science?


Based on typical score conversion charts, a raw score of 30 out of 40 converts to a scaled score of approximately 32. To hit a scaled 28, you need about 26 correct answers, meaning you can miss roughly 14 questions. Exact conversions vary slightly by test date. Check the[ACT score chart guide](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/act-score-chart-raw-to-scaled-conversion) for detailed conversion tables.


### Do I need to know actual science to do well?


For most questions, no. The section primarily tests data interpretation and scientific reasoning using information provided in the passages. However, about 4 questions per test require outside knowledge in areas like the pH scale, cell biology basics, genetics, and the scientific method.


### What is the ACT STEM Score?


The STEM Score is a new metric introduced with the Enhanced ACT. It averages your Math scaled score and your Science scaled score. It only applies if you take the optional Science section. This score is particularly relevant for students applying to STEM-focused programs.


### Should I save Conflicting Viewpoints for last?


Yes. Most test prep experts and high scorers recommend tackling Data Representation first, Research Summaries second, and Conflicting Viewpoints last. The Conflicting Viewpoints passage requires more careful reading and typically takes 6-7 minutes rather than the usual 5. Doing easier passages first builds confidence and ensures you’ve banked points before tackling the hardest section.


### How is ACT Science different from SAT Science?


The SAT does not have a standalone science section. Science-related questions on the SAT appear within the Reading and Writing section as data-analysis items, but they’re not separated into their own timed section. The ACT Science section is unique to the ACT. For a full comparison, the[SAT vs ACT guide](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/sat-vs-act-key-differences-how-to-choose) covers all the differences.


### What’s the fastest way to improve my ACT Science score?


Start with a diagnostic to identify your weakest passage types and question types. Then do daily 5-minute passage drills focused on those weak areas. Combine this with strict timing practice, and review the 18 outside-knowledge topics. Students who follow this approach consistently report gains of 4-6 points within a few weeks.
